name: Ultramontanism
summary: Ultramontanism is the nineteenth-century Catholic current that centred authority in the papacy, opposing Gallicanism and state control of the Church. It rejected liberalism, the separation of church and state and secular schooling, as set out in Pius IX's Syllabus of Errors, and backed the pope's infallibility defined at Vatican I. It is a church-political doctrine with little economic programme.
scope: The mainstream ultramontane movement of the nineteenth century, from de Maistre's Du Pape through Pius IX, the Syllabus of Errors (1864), Louis Veuillot and Manning, to Vatican I (1870). It does not cover later Catholic social teaching or post-Vatican II views. Many economic and modern issues are inferred and low confidence.

furtherReading.note: A sympathetic Catholic account of the term and its opponents.

furtherReading.title: The Syllabus of Errors
furtherReading.note: The papal text that best expresses the ultramontane stance on liberalism and the state.

keyFigures.name: Joseph de Maistre
keyFigures.role: Author of Du Pape (1819), the leading theoretical defence of papal sovereignty.

sources.title: Ultramontanism
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: Definition, opposition to Gallicanism and regalism, Vatican I, later history.

sources.title: Ultramontanism
sources.author: Umberto Benigni, The Catholic Encyclopedia (1912)
sources.usedFor: Church liberty from the state, opposition to the secular post-Revolution state, Centre party.

sources.title: The Syllabus of Errors (1864)
sources.author: Pope Pius IX
sources.usedFor: Condemned propositions on church-state separation, religious freedom, education, marriage, socialism.

sources.title: Joseph de Maistre
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: Counter-revolutionary monarchism, authority from religion, critique of rationalism.

universal-healthcare.rationale: The movement was about church authority and anti-liberalism; nineteenth-century ultramontanes left health provision to charity and the Church, and later Catholic social teaching is split on state roles.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Ultramontanism took no stand on wage law; a just-wage idea appears only in later papal social teaching, which the sources do not tie to the movement.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: The movement condemned liberalism, which included economic liberalism, but it had no economic programme; inferred from its hostility to liberal individualism.

public-ownership.rationale: The Syllabus condemns socialism and communism, so state ownership of industry would be rejected, though ultramontanes did not defend laissez-faire either.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: The movement was not concerned with taxation; adherents' views followed their social class and country.

unions-good.rationale: Ultramontanism predates Catholic labour doctrine; adherents distrusted secret societies but later favoured Catholic-run associations, so they are split.

property-fundamental.rationale: The Syllabus defends the Church's own property and condemns socialism, implying support for property rights; inferred, as property was not the movement's focus.

regulate-corporations.rationale: No ultramontane position on corporate regulation is documented; the movement's concern was ecclesiastical authority.

cut-welfare.rationale: The movement left poor relief to the Church and charity but defended no cut-welfare doctrine; adherents are split.

worker-ownership.rationale: Socialist schemes are condemned in the Syllabus; worker ownership of firms was foreign to ultramontane thought, so it is inferred as disagreement.

surveillance-ok.rationale: The issue is anachronistic; ultramontanes favoured strong authority but also complained of state intrusion on the Church.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from the movement's moral conservatism and view that law should uphold Catholic morality.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Ultramontanes demanded Church censorship of error but not 'hate speech' protections; they would condemn attacks on religion while resisting modern speech codes.

strong-leader.rationale: Ultramontanes want a strong papacy and, with de Maistre, sovereign authority, but a leader bypassing gridlock in a secular state is not their concern.

state-harmful.rationale: Ultramontanes held that civil authority is legitimate and divinely ordained; the movement defended order, not abolition of the state.

limit-guns.rationale: The issue is anachronistic and not tied to the movement.

empower-police-military.rationale: Counter-revolutionary thinkers like de Maistre prized order and authority, so more state force against revolution is inferred as agreeable.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Ultramontanes demanded that law uphold Catholic morality and condemned liberal moral permissiveness; legalised prostitution would be rejected.

decide-locally.rationale: The movement centralised authority in Rome against national and local church autonomy; for civil matters it sought no localism, though it also resisted state centralism.

rehabilitation.rationale: De Maistre defended harsh punishment, yet Catholic tradition also values reform of the sinner; adherents are split.

traditional-family.rationale: The Syllabus defends indissoluble sacramental marriage and Church jurisdiction over it, making the traditional family central to the Catholic order ultramontanes defended.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Anachronistic, but the Syllabus insists marriage is a sacrament governed by Church law; same-sex marriage would be firmly rejected.

abortion-legal.rationale: Not discussed in the Syllabus, but it is inferred from ultramontane fidelity to Catholic doctrine, which condemns abortion.

more-religion-public.rationale: Ultramontanism is integral Catholicism opposed to the secular state; it wants the Church's role in public life strengthened.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Anachronistic and outside the movement's concerns.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Inferred from Catholic natural-law anthropology that ultramontanes defended against modernism.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Ultramontanes put the universal Church above national churches and distrusted nationalism, though they defended Catholic customs in places like Quebec and Spain; split.

gradual-change.rationale: Ultramontanes respected established institutions and the Church, but in the Syllabus they rejected accommodation with modernity and sought reversal of liberal reforms.

reduce-immigration.rationale: No ultramontane position is documented; a universal Church is not hostile to migrants, yet conservatives were wary.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: The UN is anachronistic; ultramontanes did want a supranational spiritual authority in the papacy but not secular world government.

free-trade.rationale: Economic policy was not part of the movement.

nation-first.rationale: Ultramontanes were accused of being loyal to a foreign power because they placed the universal Church above national interest.

open-borders.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from the movement's preference for ordered, hierarchical society.

limit-growth.rationale: Anachronistic; ultramontanes were not degrowth thinkers though they criticised materialism.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Anachronistic and unrelated to the movement.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: The Syllabus rejects the claim that the Pope should reconcile with progress and modern civilisation; faith in progress was a liberal error.

revolution-justified.rationale: De Maistre blamed the French Revolution on rationalism, and ultramontanes opposed revolution as a rule; the Syllabus also rejects the lawfulness of rebellion.

experts-over-public.rationale: Ultramontanes favoured authority of the hierarchy over popular opinion in the Church, but not technocracy.

central-planning.rationale: Socialism is condemned in the Syllabus; centrally planned economies are inferred as rejected.

socialized-markets.rationale: Socialist models are condemned and the economy was not a movement concern; inferred disagreement.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Inferred from the movement's defence of property and family against socialism.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Industrial policy never entered ultramontane writing, which dealt with church authority rather than economic planning.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Later Catholic social teaching favours widely held property but this is not documented for the nineteenth-century movement.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Abolition of wage labour is a socialist aim, and the Syllabus condemns socialism and communism.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Monetary institutions were not an ultramontane concern, and the sources record no stance on them.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Some Catholic corporatists later drew on the tradition, yet the ultramontane movement itself did not define the position; split.

one-party-rule.rationale: The Centre party was called the Ultramontane party, showing the movement worked through party politics; rule by a single ideological party is not its model.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: De Maistre defended divine-right monarchy and the Bourbon restoration, though ultramontanism itself accepted several regimes.

democracy-best.rationale: De Maistre rejected rationalist popular sovereignty, and Pius IX condemned liberal popular-sovereignty theories; democracy was not treated as best.

direct-votes.rationale: Inferred from the hostility of de Maistre and the Church to popular sovereignty.

workers-councils.rationale: A socialist form of power rejected with socialism and communism.

right-to-secede.rationale: Not addressed; regional separation was not a movement issue.

natural-rulers.rationale: De Maistre held that sovereignty is divinely ordered and not made by the governed, and the movement held the hierarchy rules the Church by divine right.

political-violence-never.rationale: Ultramontanes did not renounce force, as de Maistre defended the executioner and states' coercion, but they opposed revolutionary violence; split leaning to disagree.

war-builds-character.rationale: De Maistre wrote of war as providential, but the movement did not teach this and the papacy preached peace.

separate-church-state.rationale: The Syllabus (section 55) condemns the proposition that Church and State should be separated.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Ultramontanes wanted Church teaching to guide law, but through natural law and papal authority, not scripture alone.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Inferred from the movement's view that authority rests on divinely sanctioned sovereigns.

ethnic-nation.rationale: The movement stressed a universal Church over national or ethnic bases.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Marxist class-conflict theory is part of the socialism the Syllabus condemns; ultramontanes saw providence and the Church as driving history.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Egalitarian levelling is inferred as rejected with socialism and the hierarchical outlook.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Indigenous land claims lie outside the movement's nineteenth-century debates over papal and state authority.

colonial-reparations.rationale: Reparations for colonialism were not discussed by ultramontane writers, so there is no documented position.

civilizational-union.rationale: The movement wanted Catholic unity under the pope, but not a political union of civilisations.

self-interest-moral.rationale: The movement condemned liberal individualism; self-interest as a moral good is contrary to Catholic ethics.

duties-before-rights.rationale: The Syllabus denies that individuals have a right to profess any religion, and stresses obedience to authority and duty.

nature-intrinsic-value.rationale: Environmental philosophy was not part of the movement, and no ultramontane source takes a side.

limit-population.rationale: Inferred from Catholic teaching on marriage and family.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Counter-revolutionaries lamented modernity's moral effects but did not call industry a disaster.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Rejects reconciliation with progress and modern civilisation, so speeding disruption is disfavoured.

human-enhancement.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from Catholic teaching on human nature.

algorithmic-government.rationale: Anachronistic; the movement's rationale for authority was divine, not technical.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: Encryption is a modern issue with no connection to the church-state disputes that defined ultramontanism.

restore-past-order.rationale: De Maistre and the ultramontanes wanted to undo the Revolution and restore Christian social order.

results-over-ideology.rationale: The movement held that doctrine and Church authority, not pragmatic results, decide, and it condemned liberal accommodation.

direct-action.rationale: Ultramontanes organised through party politics, as with the Centre party, and the Church.

means-match-ends.rationale: The movement's sources give no view on whether methods must mirror the intended society.

return-to-foraging.rationale: No ultramontane support; inferred from its civilised hierarchical Christian order.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: A radical communist aim, so rejected with communism.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Communist distribution is condemned, but Christian charity stresses care for the needy; split.

production-for-use.rationale: Ultramontanes wrote on authority and doctrine, not on the purpose of production, so adherents have no common line here.

profit-exploitation.rationale: The Marxist theory of exploitation belongs to the socialism condemned in the Syllabus.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Communism is condemned in the Syllabus; ultramontanes opposed class dictatorship.

collective-farming.rationale: Collectivisation is a communist policy and rejected.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: The Marxist theory is rejected with Marxism; ultramontanes blamed secular liberalism instead.

taxation-theft.rationale: Ultramontanes held that legitimate authority rests on divine sanction, so taxation by such authority is not theft.

harm-principle.rationale: The Syllabus rejects liberal freedom of conscience and worship, and the state may enforce Catholic morality.

individual-rights-only.rationale: The movement defended the corporate rights of the Church against the state and rejected the individualism of liberal rights.

conscription.rationale: Ultramontane sources are silent on military service; adherents could accept it under legitimate rulers.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Inferred from the movement's hierarchical idea of authority.

state-as-business.rationale: Inferred from the movement's rejection of the secular utilitarian state.

positive-liberty.rationale: The distinction between positive and negative freedom was not part of ultramontane debate, so no stance is documented.

media-academia-power.rationale: The Catholic Encyclopedia describes a coalition of rationalists and others opposed to the Church; its stance is hostile to secular press and universities, though power claims are inferred.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Not part of ultramontane teaching; Catholic doctrine held human unity.

organic-representation.rationale: Some Catholic traditionalists favoured corporate representation, but the movement is not documented on it.

total-state.rationale: Ultramontanes defended the Church's independence from state control and opposed state direction of education and culture.

national-rebirth.rationale: Ultramontanes sought restoration of Christian order rather than a national palingenesis, and the sources record no position.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Not part of the movement's aims; it defended the papal states, not conquest.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Feudal oaths of personal loyalty are not discussed in the movement's sources, though loyalty to the pope was central in Church matters.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Ultramontanes held that truth is objective and held by the Church, not constructed by power, though they argued that secular teaching served error.

universal-morality.rationale: The movement defended Catholic natural-law teaching as binding truth for all, against relativism condemned in the Syllabus.

single-common-good.rationale: Ultramontanes thought politics should serve a single Catholic order of truth rather than balance interests, an inference from integral Catholicism.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: Diaspora citizenship rights were not an ultramontane topic, so no position is documented.

revive-national-language.rationale: Not addressed; Latin and Roman unity were more important.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Inferred from rejection of socialism and of democratic principles.

school-vouchers.rationale: Ultramontanes demanded Church control of schooling and opposed state monopoly (Syllabus sections 45-47), which public funding of Church schools would serve.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Fiscal policy was outside the movement's concerns and the sources record no position.

economic-freedom.rationale: Economic liberalism was not a movement doctrine and liberalism was condemned.

rule-by-example.rationale: De Maistre stressed authority sanctioned by religion and punishment alongside example; split.

national-self-determination.rationale: The movement defended the Papal States and Church supremacy over nationalism, so it did not accept self-determination as a general right.

force-without-un.rationale: The UN postdates the movement, which had no doctrine on authorising force beyond just-war teaching.

reason-over-faith.rationale: De Maistre held that rationalist justification of authority undermines it, and the Syllabus condemns rationalism.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: Welfare entitlements for immigrants were not an ultramontane issue; the Church ran charity itself.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Work requirements for welfare were not discussed by ultramontanes, who left relief largely to Church charity.

class-collaboration.rationale: Opposed to class conflict and socialism; the Catholic view is of harmony between orders, though the movement did not elaborate it.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: The movement was about conserving inherited institutions and rejected the break with tradition.

dominated-front.rationale: A common front of Western-dominated countries has no counterpart in ultramontane thought.

workers-nation.rationale: The question of whether workers organise nationally or internationally is a socialist debate absent from ultramontane writing.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: The Syllabus's defence of traditional marriage and family implies distinct roles; the movement did not legislate on it.

ban-interest.rationale: Canon law once condemned usury, but nineteenth-century Catholics had accepted lending; split.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Not a movement position; Catholic doctrine affirms common humanity.

state-class-instrument.rationale: A Marxist claim rejected in the Syllabus's condemnation of socialism; ultramontanes saw authority as divinely based.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Energy policy is a modern matter on which ultramontane sources are silent.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Immigrant assimilation was not a theme of the movement, which stressed a universal Church over national culture.

proportional-representation.rationale: Electoral systems were not a concern of the movement, which was suspicious of popular sovereignty itself.

national-mission.rationale: The movement saw the Church, not a nation, as having a universal mission.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Inferred; the movement affirmed traditional hierarchy and would not call it injustice.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Ultramontanes attacked liberal and anticlerical politicians but did not frame the political class as corrupt in general.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Eugenic coercion contradicts Catholic teaching on marriage and the person.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Legal accountability for past state killings is a modern transitional-justice question with no ultramontane position.

night-watchman-state.rationale: The movement wanted the state to uphold Catholic religion and morals, not be a minimal state.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Contrary to Catholic teaching on marriage; not a movement position.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Catholic doctrine of equal souls applies, but the Syllabus rejects liberal legal equality of religions, so confidence is low.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: Settler colonialism as a category is modern and was not addressed by ultramontane writers.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: The Syllabus rejects civil jurisdiction over marriage and subordination of Church law, which a uniform civil code would imply.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Ultramontanes wanted Catholic establishment and Protestant proselytism restrained (section 77 on religion of the state), but not a general conversion law; split.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: The Syllabus (sections 45-47) condemns state control of schools free of Church authority.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Ultramontanes and de Maistre located legitimacy in divine sanction, not in popular consent.

trade-surplus.rationale: Mercantilist trade goals were outside the ultramontane agenda, and no source gives a position.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Ultramontane thinkers like de Maistre accepted state coercion and war as providential, so an absolute ban on initiating force is not theirs; inferred.

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Social Darwinist ideas conflict with Catholic ethics and with the Syllabus's rejection of unchecked progress.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Ultramontanes were themselves targeted by bans during the Kulturkampf and would object to such powers in anticlerical hands.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: The republican theory of freedom was not part of ultramontane debates, so no position is documented.

separated-powers.rationale: Ultramontanes favoured a Church independent of state, a type of dual authority, but did not endorse constitutional separation of powers in general.

vanguard-party.rationale: A communist doctrine, condemned with communism.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Charity was central to Catholicism but the movement did not make it a legal priority.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: Council housing is a twentieth-century British policy outside the movement's period.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Strike law was not debated in ultramontane sources, and adherents had no shared view.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: Inferred from Catholic opposition to Malthusian ideas.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Ultramontane writing treated religious unity, not ethnic diversity, as the basis of cohesion, so no direct position is documented.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Inferred from the movement's view that authority is divinely sanctioned, not random.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Counter-revolutionary thought valued order, but the movement was not documented on emergency powers.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Price controls on food were not a topic for the movement, and adherents had no common view.

party-controls-media.rationale: Ultramontanes opposed state control of the press as an attack on Church independence, though they sought Church censorship of error.

party-commands-army.rationale: Party control of armed forces is alien to the movement.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Naturalisation periods were not an ultramontane concern.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Pay for legislators was not discussed by the movement, so no position is recorded.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: The Centre party worked as a bloc under the Church, but the principle is not defined in the sources.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Supranational unions such as the EU postdate the movement, which only sought a universal spiritual authority in the papacy.

head-commands-forces.rationale: De Maistre favoured strong monarchy, but no explicit view on this.

church-by-bishops.rationale: The movement held that the church is governed by the hierarchy under the pope, and not by congregations or assemblies.

clerical-rule.rationale: Ultramontanes claimed papal authority over spiritual and some civil affairs, but in practice defended Church liberty rather than rule by clergy; split.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: A Leninist doctrine; revolutionary defeatism contradicts counter-revolutionary politics.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: The Syllabus and the movement supported Church censorship of error and condemned the claim that free expression doesn't harm morals (section 79).

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Term limits for presidents were not part of the movement's concerns.

recall-officials.rationale: Inferred from rejection of popular-sovereignty institutions.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Military alliances were not discussed in ultramontane sources, so there is no documented position.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Inferred; property was defended against socialism.

people-in-arms.rationale: Inferred from the movement's order and authority emphasis.

rural-life-healthier.rationale: Counter-revolutionary Catholic writers contrasted rural piety with urban secularism, but this is inferred.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: The movement's territorial concern was the Papal States, not reunification of divided nations in general.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Ultramontanes opposed secular universities, but the claim as stated is not documented.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: The movement held Catholic Christendom to be the true civilisation and the Syllabus rejects equality of religions.

death-penalty.rationale: De Maistre defended capital punishment and the executioner's role in the social order, and the Papal States used it.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: The Syllabus rejects state control of schooling and moral teaching apart from the Church.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: The Syllabus resists secular science overriding Church teaching (section 12), but the movement did not demand creationism; split.

restrict-pornography.rationale: The movement wanted law to support Catholic morals and condemned the claim that unrestricted expression is harmless (section 79).

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: The rules for passing citizenship were not an ultramontane topic.

minority-language-support.rationale: Minority language policy is not discussed in the sources, though Latin liturgy was prized.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Ultramontanes defended the Church's liberty from state interference and sought exemptions for Catholics, e.g. in the Kulturkampf, though minority protection generally was not their theme.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Mill-style individual liberty is the liberalism condemned in the Syllabus.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: Third-world debt cancellation is a modern issue that ultramontanism never addressed.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: This anti-colonial claim has no counterpart in the movement's concerns.

constituent-assembly.rationale: Popular constitution-making conflicts with the Syllabus's rejection of popular sovereignty.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Developmentalist trade-offs of freedom for growth were not addressed by the movement.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Charity is a Catholic duty, but the movement's sources set out no doctrine of international aid.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: Nuclear weapons postdate the movement, so no position is documented.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Inferred from preference for monarchy and divine legitimacy.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Central banking policy was not part of the ultramontane agenda.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Ultramontanes defended the pope's territories (the Papal States) against surrender, which supports this as a principle.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Catholic doctrine holds property has a social function, but nineteenth-century ultramontanes stressed property rights against socialism; low confidence.

soviet-state-capitalist.rationale: The debate over the nature of the Soviet Union postdates the movement.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Environmental regulation doctrine is modern and unaddressed in ultramontane sources.

collective-defense.rationale: Alliance guarantees such as NATO's postdate the movement, and no stance is documented.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: The movement viewed the annexation of the Papal States as unlawful, but a general principle is not set out.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: The Syllabus condemns placing the clergy under civil authority and state control of Church property and rights (for example sections 19, 24, 41-42).

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Ultramontane sources do not discuss the ceremonial role of a head of state, though it fits papal ideas of a ruler above faction.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Ultramontane writing does not address secession, though it defended the Papal States against annexation.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Special autonomy arrangements for regions were not addressed by the movement.

sacred-ruler.rationale: De Maistre saw sovereignty as divinely sanctioned, though not as divine descent; Catholic doctrine rejects ruler divinity.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Income tax structure was outside the movement's concerns.

character-from-environment.rationale: The movement affirmed original sin and moral nature, not environmental determinism.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: De Maistre saw sovereigns as bound by divine law and the pope's authority over rulers; the Church's claim of papal supremacy limits rulers.

space-expansion.rationale: Space exploration postdates the movement, and no stance is documented.

mixed-constitution.rationale: De Maistre favoured monarchy but acknowledged mixed forms like Britain's; not a defining view.

leader-cult.rationale: The papal cult of personality arose within Church, but civil leader worship contradicts Catholic teaching; split in practice.

equal-parenting.rationale: Custody rules after separation are a modern matter, and divorce itself was condemned by the movement.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: A Maoist idea outside ultramontane thought; rejected with Marxism.

land-redistribution.rationale: Seizure of estates is socialist-style expropriation, and the Syllabus defends property and Church holdings.

refugee-return.rationale: Refugee return rights were not an ultramontane topic.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: The Syllabus defends Catholic state religion but nineteenth-century ultramontanes did not uniformly seek legal punishment for apostasy; split.

common-currency.rationale: Monetary union was not discussed by the movement, so no position is documented.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: The movement valued a universal Church over ethnic unity.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Minority cultural autonomy within states was not a theme of ultramontane writing.

rights-where-you-live.rationale: Debates over minority emigration versus integration were not part of the movement's discourse.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: De Maistre and ultramontanes held that ideas, religion and providence drive history, and blamed the Revolution on rationalism.

ban-cartels.rationale: Competition policy was not addressed by ultramontane writers.

no-bailouts.rationale: Bailouts of banks or firms were not an ultramontane topic.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Ultramontanes rejected majority sovereignty as supreme and held a higher divine law binds states.

gender-parity-bodies.rationale: Inferred from traditional views of roles.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Autarkic bloc economics were absent from the movement's concerns.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: Binding trade standards are a modern policy and no ultramontane source addresses them.

moral-incentives.rationale: The movement made no statement about replacing material incentives, though Catholic moral teaching values duty.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Revolution is the evil the movement opposed.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: De Maistre defended hereditary monarchy and aristocracy and ultramontanes sided with the old order.

missingStatements.text: The pope should have the final authority in matters of faith and morals for the whole Church.
missingStatements.rationale: Papal primacy and infallibility, defined at Vatican I, are the defining ultramontane claim, opposed by Gallicans.
missingStatements.declined: Specific to papal doctrine of the Catholic Church; too narrow for a question many ideologies take sides on, and church-governance stances are covered by church-by-bishops and clerical-rule.

missingStatements.text: Civil rulers should have no authority over the internal governance of a church.
missingStatements.rationale: Ultramontanes opposed Gallicanism, Josephinism and regalism by insisting on the Church's independence from the state.

missingStatements.text: Marriage should be governed by religious law rather than by the civil courts.
missingStatements.rationale: The Syllabus condemns the propositions that civil contract suffices for marriage and that matrimonial cases belong to civil tribunals (sections 73-74).

notes: Ultramontanism is a church-political movement; economic and modern issues are mostly inferred, so many answers are low or neutral. Some statements are repeated in the answer source only once.
